tldr: We propose PAMORT, a multi-objective reinforcement learning framework that enables a quadrupedal robot to carry unsecured stacked cardboard boxes on a flat board across uneven terrain without dedicated payload sensors or active mechanisms. By adapting the trade-off between locomotion speed and payload stability online using only proprioception, it achieves high transportation success rates in real-world experiments.
hero_caption: A quadrupedal robot (Unitree Go2) transporting unsecured stacked boxes on a flat carrier board. Even though it was trained only on a two-box stack in simulation, it traverses real-world uneven terrains such as grass, slopes, and steps, generalizing zero-shot to an unseen three-box stack and side-by-side payload configurations.
overview:
Quadrupedal locomotion has advanced dramatically. Legged robots can now traverse challenging uneven terrains such as stairs and steep slopes. However, for practical transportation in warehouses or construction sites, conventional approaches that rigidly strap payloads down or use walled containers and dedicated manipulators introduce significant operational overhead and costs for loading and unloading. In this paper, the authors tackle an extremely challenging task: transporting unsecured, stacked cardboard boxes placed on a completely flat, edgeless board across uneven terrain.

When payloads are not secured, aggressive acceleration or ground impacts can cause boxes to slide or collapse, even if the robot itself remains perfectly stable. In other words, there is a strong trade-off between moving fast to track velocity commands and keeping the payload steady to prevent falls. To resolve this, the authors developed PAMORT (Payload-Adaptive Multi-Objective Reinforcement learning for Transportation), a two-phase reinforcement learning framework. First, they train a multi-objective base policy conditioned on a preference vector that weights locomotion and payload stability. Second, they train a weight adjuster on the frozen policy to dynamically adapt this preference online using only the robot's proprioception.

Using a Unitree Go2, the authors evaluated the system across eight rough-terrain courses, including slopes and steps that match or exceed the training difficulty. PAMORT achieved an overall mean success rate of 0.850, substantially outperforming a single-objective baseline (0.675). Furthermore, it exhibited robust zero-shot generalization to an unseen three-box stack configuration that was never experienced during training.
contributions: Achieved uneven-terrain transportation of unsecured stacked payloads using only standard quadruped leg joints and proprioception, without dedicated payload sensors or external active mechanisms.

Proposed PAMORT, a two-phase framework consisting of a multi-objective policy conditioned on a preference vector to balance locomotion and payload stability, paired with a weight adjuster that adapts this preference online.

Introduced a preference-aware curriculum that aggregates locomotion and payload progress using a geometric mean, ensuring conservative policies advance through terrain difficulty levels appropriately.

Demonstrated strong generalization and high success rates in simulation and on a physical Unitree Go2 across terrains harsher than training and unseen payload configurations, such as a three-box stack.

sections.heading: Carrying Without Straps: The Locomotion–Payload Dilemma for Quadruped Robots
sections.summary: Quadrupeds hold great promise for logistics, but rigid mechanical fixturing limits operational flexibility. Transporting unsecured stacked boxes requires whole-body coordination to prevent collapses alongside robot stability, creating an inherent trade-off between velocity tracking and payload protection. This work proposes PAMORT to resolve this trade-off online via multi-objective reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
Quadrupedal robots can access uneven terrains where wheeled platforms fail. As a result, they have attracted strong interest for material transport in logistics and construction. However, most existing approaches assume payloads are bolted, strapped, or enclosed in walled containers. While secure, this requires specialized fixtures and cumbersome loading/unloading procedures for each payload type, sacrificing operational flexibility.

To address this, the authors explore transporting cardboard boxes loosely stacked on an edgeless, flat board mounted on the robot's torso across rough terrain. Without fixtures, even if the robot walks stably, foot impacts or rapid accelerations easily cause the boxes to slip or topple. Keeping the payload stable requires more than simply holding the torso level; it demands coordinated whole-body motions, such as actively tilting the torso during acceleration and deceleration.

This introduces a fundamental trade-off between locomotion performance and payload stability. Aggressively pursuing velocity commands risks toppling the boxes. Conversely, overly prioritizing payload safety leads to stalling or excessively sluggish motion. To balance these conflicting demands autonomously without extra sensors, the authors turn to multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) to arbitrate the trade-off online.

captions.F1: Overview of unsecured stacked payload transportation on an edgeless board. In addition to simulation (A), real-world tests on a Unitree Go2 cover diverse terrains including wavy grass (B), up-slopes (C), down-slopes (D), and step obstacles (E, F).

sections.heading: Legged Transport and Multi-Objective RL: Moving Beyond Rigid Fixtures
sections.summary: Prior legged transport studies mostly assume rigid attachment or rely on external manipulators and tactile sensors for unsecured objects. Meanwhile, multi-objective RL (MORL) with preference conditioning has advanced for managing trade-offs within a single policy. This paper uniquely adapts MORL preferences online from proprioception alone under partial observability where the payload cannot be directly measured.
sections.details:
### Payload Transportation with Legged Robots
Most prior research on legged payload transport assumes the cargo is rigidly attached to the robot or enclosed in containers. The primary challenge was maintaining stable locomotion against variations in total mass, center of mass, and inertia. For unsecured loads, existing works have demonstrated ball-balancing on flat plates, active stabilization via torso-mounted arms, or monitoring contact states via tactile sensors (such as LocoTouch). However, these require dedicated actuators or extra sensors. Stacked boxes introduce coupled sliding and toppling dynamics between layers, yet solving this purely through leg locomotion without extra hardware has remained largely unexplored.

### Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning (MORL)
Standard RL collapses multiple objectives into a single scalar reward using fixed weights, whereas MORL explicitly handles trade-offs among objectives. In particular, preference-conditioned MORL feeds a preference vector into the policy, allowing a single policy to generate a spectrum of behaviors suitable for robot control. Recent works have applied dynamic preference adaptation to tasks such as character animation tracking (e.g., AMOR). Building upon this concept, this paper introduces a key novelty: adapting the preference online using solely the robot's onboard proprioception, under partial observability where payload states cannot be measured directly via cameras or force sensors.

sections.heading: Two-Phase Training and Reward Design: How PAMORT Arbitrates Speed and Stability
sections.summary: PAMORT is trained in two phases building on Teacher-Actor-Critic (TAR). Phase 1 trains a multi-objective base policy conditioned on locomotion and payload weights using a preference-aware curriculum. Phase 2 freezes this policy and trains a weight adjuster (WA). Tailored reward terms penalize misalignment and unnecessary planar acceleration while actively promoting restorative maneuvers.
sections.details:
### Phase 1: Training the Multi-Objective Base Policy
The foundation is built on TAR, an asymmetric actor-critic framework. During training, privileged information (exact payload positions, velocities, physical parameters) is provided to the teacher encoder and critic, which is distilled via contrastive learning into a student encoder that uses only proprioception. PAMORT augments the actor input with a 2D preference vector $\boldsymbol{w}_t = [w_t^{\mathrm{move}}, w_t^{\mathrm{payload}}]^\top$ and extends the critic into a multi-head structure corresponding to both reward groups.

- Reward Grouping and Sampling: Rewards are cleanly split into a move group and a payload group. During training, the preference vector $\boldsymbol{w}$ is uniformly sampled per episode from a Dirichlet distribution $\mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,1)$.
- Multi-Objective PPO: Rewards in each group are normalized using running statistics to compute separate advantages, which are then combined into a scalar advantage $\tilde{A}_t = \boldsymbol{w}^\top \boldsymbol{A}_t$ to update the policy.
- Preference-Aware Curriculum: Traditional terrain curricula based purely on traveled distance misinterpret careful, slow walking aimed at payload safety as poor learning progress. To fix this, competence is defined as the weighted geometric mean of normalized move progress $c_{\mathrm{move}}$ and time-to-first-drop progress $c_{\mathrm{payload}}$: $c_{\mathrm{agg}} = c_{\mathrm{move}}^{w^{\mathrm{move}}} \cdot c_{\mathrm{payload}}^{w^{\mathrm{payload}}}$, ensuring terrains advance appropriately across all preferences.

### Phase 2: Training the Weight Adjuster (WA)
With the trained multi-objective policy completely frozen, a higher-level policy—the Weight Adjuster (WA)—is trained. The WA reads current proprioceptive states and outputs the preference vector $\boldsymbol{w}_t$ at a lower frequency than the base policy (every 4 steps, or $0.08\,\mathrm{s}$). A smoothness loss on consecutive weight changes prevents sudden behavioral shifts that could destabilize the boxes.

### Specialized Reward Formulation
Four dedicated terms stabilize the payload:
- Alignment Rewards: Penalize horizontal offset of the bottom box from the board center, as well as the top box from the bottom box.
- Planar Acceleration Penalties: Merely penalizing acceleration prevents the robot from restoring shifted boxes. Instead, the framework computes the difference between planar gravity components and payload acceleration, penalizing deviation from a target restoring acceleration $\boldsymbol{u}_\star^i$ toward the board center. This cancels inertial forces during speed changes while encouraging the robot to tilt and slide shifted boxes back to the center.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of PAMORT. In Phase 1 (top), a multi-objective policy is trained under random preference weights $w_t$. In Phase 2 (bottom), the student encoder and policy are frozen, and the Weight Adjuster is trained to output optimal $w_t$ values in real time from proprioception.

sections.heading: Simulation Setup: Distilling Privileged State and Domain Randomization for Sim-to-Real
sections.summary: Training is conducted in Isaac Lab on a Unitree Go2. Phase 1 uses 16,384 parallel environments with 10 terrain levels and extensive domain randomization. During physical deployment, no privileged payload or terrain data is used; control relies exclusively on proprioceptive states such as joint positions and velocities.
sections.details:
### Simulation Environment
Isaac Lab is used as the simulation platform. A $0.4\,\mathrm{m} \times 0.4\,\mathrm{m}$ edgeless carrier board with a thickness of $0.02\,\mathrm{m}$ is mounted on the Unitree Go2 torso. The single-objective baseline (TAR*) and Phase 2 WA training utilize 8,192 environments across 4 GPUs, while Phase 1 multi-objective training uses 16,384 environments across 8 GPUs to adequately cover the extra preference dimension. The control frequency is $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$ ($20\,\mathrm{ms}$ step), with a maximum episode length of $20\,\mathrm{s}$.

### Proprioceptive vs. Privileged Observations
At deployment, the actor receives only a 45-dimensional proprioceptive vector containing base angular velocity, projected gravity, target velocity commands, joint positions, joint velocities, and the previous action. In contrast, the training-time teacher encoder and critic access a 195-dimensional privileged vector including ground-truth robot states, contact forces, local terrain height scans, linear acceleration, and exact positions, velocities, and physical parameters of both boxes. The student encoder reconstructs these privileged latent representations using a 1-layer LSTM (hidden size 256) tracking proprioceptive history.

### Domain Randomization
To achieve successful zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, comprehensive domain randomization is applied. Masses, inertias, and friction coefficients of both robot and boxes are randomized across wide ranges. Additionally, intermittent planar velocity disturbances are applied to the robot torso and each box during locomotion, fostering robustness against unexpected real-world shocks.

captions.F4: Representative terrain types at difficulty level 6 used in simulation evaluation. Diverse terrains include random rough, rough blocks, fine blocks, slopes, wide stairs, and narrow stairs.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Pareto Optimality and Dominant Real-World Go2 Performance
sections.summary: In simulation, PAMORT maps a continuous Pareto front within a single policy and surpasses the TAR* baseline in success rate via online weight adjustment. In real-world Go2 experiments spanning harsh slopes, steps, and an unseen three-box stack, PAMORT achieves a mean success rate of 0.850, well ahead of the baseline's 0.675.
sections.details:
### Pareto Analysis of the Base Policy
The authors first verified that the Phase 1 policy captures the intended trade-off. Evaluating 21 values of $w^{\mathrm{payload}}$ from $0.0$ to $1.0$ revealed a clean non-dominated Pareto front over $0.4 \le w^{\mathrm{payload}} \le 1.0$. Its performance matched or exceeded four separate TAR* baselines trained individually with fixed weights, confirming that a single multi-objective model can master diverse behavioral modes.

### Simulation Evaluation
The full PAMORT pipeline (with WA) was tested across 9 terrain types spanning difficulty levels 0 to 9 (levels 7 to 9 exceed training bounds). Tests covered the trained two-box setup, as well as zero-box, one-box, and an unseen three-box configuration. PAMORT surpassed TAR* in average success rate across all payload settings. Furthermore, compared to an "oracle" baseline that retrospectively picks the best fixed weight for each setting, PAMORT reached roughly 95–96% of oracle performance without any prior search.

### Real-World Go2 Deployment
Physical tests used pallet-constructed ramps (38%, 44% slopes) and step obstacles ($16\,\mathrm{cm}$, $20\,\mathrm{cm}$). The 44% slope and both step obstacles exceeded the maximum training difficulty (40% slope, $15\,\mathrm{cm}$ step).
- Two-box stack: PAMORT outperformed the baseline in 3 out of 4 environments, scoring a mean success rate of 0.875 versus 0.650 for TAR*.
- Unseen three-box stack: PAMORT maintained an average success rate of 0.825, far exceeding TAR* (0.700).
- Across all eight tasks, PAMORT averaged 0.850, compared to 0.675 for TAR*.

Behavioral logs reveal that $w^{\mathrm{payload}}$ drops to around 0.5–0.7 on flat ground to gain forward momentum, then spikes to 0.8–0.95 when facing steep ascents or step drops to carefully stabilize cargo. The robot dynamically tilts its torso pitch during accelerations and decelerations to prevent box slippage. Inference takes only $0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$ on the robot, well within the $20\,\mathrm{ms}$ control budget.

captions.F3: Empirical Pareto front showing the trade-off between locomotion and payload rewards. PAMORT (circles) traces a smooth front as $w^{\mathrm{payload}}$ varies, encompassing separately trained fixed-weight TAR* baselines (black stars, squares, etc.) within a single policy.
captions.F6: Trajectories of payload weight $w^{\mathrm{payload}}$ and torso pitch during a real Go2 trial on a 44% ramp with two boxes. At difficult transitions (slope entry and step landing), the weight automatically climbs toward 0.9, and the robot tilts its torso forward and backward to counteract slippage.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook: Sensor-Free Transport Toward Many-Objective RL
sections.summary: This study demonstrated through PAMORT that a quadruped can transport unsecured stacked loads over uneven terrain using only proprioception. While it shows remarkable robustness across unseen terrains and box configurations, expanding to deformable objects, liquids, and many-objective RL formulations with four or more goals represents the next frontier.
sections.details:
This work introduced PAMORT, a framework for quadrupedal transport of unsecured stacked payloads on rough terrain. By combining a preference-conditioned multi-objective base policy with a proprioceptive weight adjuster, the system reconciles the conflicting demands of tracking velocity and preventing payload collapse without any payload sensors or external manipulators.

Physical trials on a Unitree Go2 demonstrated zero-shot transfer to severe slopes, steps, and an unseen three-box stack beyond training limits, reaching an overall success rate of 0.850 and significantly outperforming the baseline.

However, the authors note limitations: payloads are restricted to rigid cuboid boxes, and objectives are limited to two groups (locomotion and payload). Future work aims to tackle irregular, deformable items and sloshing liquids, as well as scaling to many-objective reinforcement learning with four or more goals (such as energy efficiency and safety), marking vital steps toward practical robotic transportation.

takeaways: Even without sensors looking at the cargo, the robot's proprioceptive history (foot impacts, joint loads, base orientation) provides sufficient information to detect destabilization and adjust posture and stepping online.

Instead of settling for a fixed-weight compromise between competing goals (speed vs. cargo safety), training a preference-conditioned multi-objective policy and steering weights via a higher-level adjuster preserves the Pareto frontier effectively.

The preference-aware curriculum design—combining objective-specific progress via a weighted geometric mean—prevents cautious, slow behaviors from being penalized as stalled learning, offering a practical blueprint for multi-objective RL.
limitations: The study only investigates rigid rectangular cardboard boxes; direct applicability to irregular objects, deformable bodies, or sloshing liquids remains untested.

The reward structure is restricted to two groups (a 1D simplex between locomotion and payload); expanding to three or more objectives, such as energy efficiency or joint torque limits, exponentially increases the difficulty of learning Pareto-optimal solutions.
